sections.title: Declare exact instrument grids
sections.explanation: The configuration names BTC-USDT and ETH-USDT with quoted decimal tick and lot sizes. Display precisions are explicit and agree with those grids. The quoted decimal values preserve the intended boundary representation for later exact instrument conversion.

sections.title: Set timing and FIX ownership
sections.explanation: Network delay is zero and engine delay is one simulated millisecond, with deterministic random seed 42 and no simulated random rejection. The administration API binds to loopback on port 8001, and FIX delivery has explicit retry-cycle and retained-record limits. The exact stable FIX session string maps to a participant identity, separating transport identity from ownership policy.

sections.title: Require explicit time advancement
sections.explanation: The scheduler uses external mode, so queued work progresses through explicit advancement rather than an elapsed wall-clock loop. Maximum advance duration and event count bound administrative requests. These limits are part of the run’s execution policy and should be read alongside inclusive target handling in the scheduler.

sections.title: Bound streaming and expose metrics
sections.explanation: WebSocket settings specify queue capacity, send timeout, heartbeat/staleness thresholds, fallback polling, and reconnect backoff. The empty CORS-origin list grants no extra cross-origin browser access. Prometheus is enabled on the application service rather than configured as a separate listener here.

sections.title: Keep native feeds optional
sections.explanation: ITCH and GLIMPSE are disabled in this local profile, while their metadata and SoupBinTCP settings remain visible for deliberate configuration. The Soup section supplies listener, login, write, connection, and bounded replay-cache values. Its CHANGE_ME credential is an example configuration value; enabling recovery also requires the corresponding coherent native feed configuration.

Health dependencies turn the earlier startup and readiness concepts into a runnable service graph.

sections.title: Persistent QuestDB service
sections.explanation: QuestDB uses a pinned image, a named data volume, and explicit HTTP and PostgreSQL credentials. Automatic creation of tables and columns from line-protocol traffic is disabled, leaving schema management to the application adapter. The authenticated health check must pass before the dependent MockX service starts.

sections.title: Exchange configuration and readiness
sections.explanation: MockX uses the local application image and concrete exchange and FIX configuration paths. Persistence environment variables set ingestion endpoints, bounded record and byte capacity, flush cadence, retry limits, shutdown timeout, and rejection of new records on overflow. Published ports expose FIX, HTTP, and local TCP recovery, while `/readyz` supplies the health gate used by the downstream demo services.

sections.title: Multicast relay to the host
sections.explanation: The relay reuses the application image and runs the MoldUDP64 host-relay example with a configured multicast group and port. Its destination is `host.docker.internal`, allowing the demo to forward native feed traffic toward a host-side consumer. It starts after MockX is healthy and restarts on failure.

sections.title: Continuous demo traffic
sections.explanation: The live-market service runs the FIX driver with the Docker exchange and client configuration files. Its application URL uses the Compose service address, while the UI URL points to the host-published HTTP port. Startup waits for healthy MockX and a started relay; SIGTERM and a thirty-second grace period provide the driver a defined shutdown window.

Dockerfile.overview: The image packages the Python exchange and its runtime assets on Python 3.11 slim. It installs dependencies before copying frequently changed source, then runs the CLI as a dedicated unprivileged user. The deployment tour step pairs this image recipe with Compose settings that provide configuration and optional surrounding services.

sections.title: Base and dependency installation
sections.explanation: The build starts from Python 3.11 slim and installs system build tools, Git, and curl before cleaning the apt package lists. requirements.txt is copied and installed before application source, so source-only changes can reuse the dependency layer. The working directory is fixed at /opt/mockx for subsequent assets and execution.

sections.title: Assets and runtime ownership
sections.explanation: The image copies source, templates, examples, and the FIX dictionary, then creates log and store directories. A dedicated trader account is given ownership of the application directory and selected as the runtime user. These filesystem choices provide the relative assets and writable paths expected by the packaged application.

sections.title: CLI runtime contract
sections.explanation: CFG_PATH provides the conventional mounted configuration location, and PYTHONPATH exposes the copied source tree. The entry point invokes the CLI as a Python module, so argument parsing and configuration validation follow the same path as a direct launch. Deployment supplies the actual configuration file at runtime.

It combines paced FIX submission, ledger settlement, observed depth, optional midpoint correction, probes, and final feed reconciliation. The Historical Market Replay tour step uses it to show how the exchange contracts are exercised through actual interfaces rather than direct book mutation.

sections.title: Project wall time into replay time
sections.explanation: ClockProjection maps monotonic wall timestamps to simulated replay timestamps and performs the inverse deadline calculation for pacing. ReplayOptions limits rate to a finite value in (0, 1] and validates positive durations, lag limits, and pending capacity. Slower playback therefore scales the timing relationship explicitly instead of merely sleeping longer between arbitrary batches.

sections.title: Bound submission and settle reports
sections.explanation: Submission enforces a pending-request cap and records dispatch lag against the projected deadline. Report handling distinguishes historical ledger orders from external controller or probe activity, sharing cumulative-fill watermarks across related cancellation identities. Explicit rejections and overdue unresolved outcomes fail the experiment instead of allowing a superficially completed replay with missing acknowledgements.

sections.title: Observe quality without changing history
sections.explanation: New feed sequences update the controller with exact depth and both market and receive timing. Quality samples compare the current historical reference with observed midpoint, spread, and top-ten quantity. Statistics polling verifies run ownership and scheduler health, records round-trip timing, and rejects excessive scheduler lag.

sections.title: Manage independent probe lifetimes
sections.explanation: The optional strategy probe sends a small IOC sweep plus a passive GTC order using a separate actor identity. A later cancellation is sent only while that passive identity remains tracked as live external work. The pending-cancel marker prevents generating another probe pair before the prior probe cycle has been handled.

sections.title: Seed and establish the timing anchor
sections.explanation: The runner registers historical snapshot orders, starts FIX sessions, and submits the seed through the session-start administration contract. It starts market-data observation and waits for the realtime scheduler to catch up before estimating a wall/simulation clock anchor from a statistics round trip. Only then does it initialize the historical iterator and target midpoint for paced playback.

sections.title: Release due work fairly
sections.explanation: Each loop first processes reports and observations, then retries only per-order dependencies that were deferred by the ledger. The release loop refreshes the current clock for each due event and caps a batch at 128 events; lag and backlog bounds remain explicit failures. One asynchronous statistics request is allowed at a time, and the final sleep yields immediately when source work is already due instead of adding an unnecessary timer delay.

sections.title: Fence the final observable state
sections.explanation: At the end of playback, the controller stops and outstanding probes and FIX responses are drained. A transport fence establishes that prior session traffic has been processed before the runner compares the final REST book with the WebSocket observation. When the native probe is enabled, its sequence and depth must also agree before the result becomes completed.

sections.title: Retain results through cleanup
sections.explanation: Failures and cancellation are recorded in the result before being re-raised. The finally block records bounded timing, actor-fill, accuracy, memory, and feed summaries, then ends only the generation owned by this runner. Cleanup errors are collected separately and can downgrade a previously completed result to failed, so successful playback cannot hide resource or lifecycle shutdown failure.

examples/coinapi_replay/source.py.overview: ReplaySource turns a local CoinAPI L3 CSV capture into an initial order snapshot followed by a single stream of exact source events. It preserves nanosecond timestamps, instrument ticks and lots, and distinct order lifetimes while maintaining historical reference depth. This is the input-side contract used by the replay runner to compare exchange behavior with only the source state reached so far.

sections.title: Immutable source records and time
sections.explanation: Frozen source-order and source-event records distinguish the raw source ID from a lifetime-qualified ID and retain quantities in lots. Timestamp parsing handles up to nine fractional digits using integer arithmetic, with a date requirement for time-only values. An explicitly asserted date is checked against capture filename metadata instead of silently choosing between conflicting dates.

sections.title: Exact reference price levels
sections.explanation: The reference book stores integer aggregate quantities alongside sorted price lists. Changes update both structures and reject quantity underflow, removing a price when its quantity reaches zero. Its midpoint is represented as twice the midpoint in ticks, avoiding fractional arithmetic, and locked or crossed source books are rejected as unsupported discontinuities.

sections.title: Initial snapshot boundary
sections.explanation: Construction detects comma or semicolon CSV, requires the expected L3 columns, and consumes the opening SNAPSHOT rows eagerly. Those rows must agree on both timestamps, and the first subsequent increment is retained for later iteration. The resulting immutable seed snapshot is therefore established without applying future increments to the live reference state.

sections.title: Row validation and conversion
sections.explanation: Parsing checks field counts, source-symbol consistency, nondecreasing exchange time, supported operations, side flags, and nonempty order IDs. Instrument helpers convert prices and quantities into exact tick and lot units. Zero quantity is admitted only for the deletion or SET cases that can represent removal, and parse failures carry the original row ordinal.

sections.title: Order lifetimes and increments
sections.explanation: SNAPSHOT and ADD create a new lifetime-qualified source identity and reject an already live raw ID. Other actions require that live identity and its unchanged side and price, then apply subtraction, matching, setting, or deletion while tracking historical matched lots. Aggregate reference depth changes by the exact quantity delta, and terminal lifetimes are removed so a later raw-ID reuse becomes a distinct source order.

sections.title: Single-pass consumption and depth
sections.explanation: Events can be consumed only once, and a later SNAPSHOT is rejected because it requires a new replay segment. Each yielded increment first updates the reference book, event count, and final timestamp; `reference_depth` exposes only this reached state with bids descending and asks ascending. The context manager opens only local CSV or gzipped CSV input and closes its stream when replay consumption finishes.

In Native Consumers and Routing, this file shows how a downstream client turns transport loss into explicit recovery rather than silently applying an incomplete sequence.

sections.title: Receive into bounded storage
sections.explanation: UdpReceiver reserves ring slots and commits complete datagrams for the consumer. When capacity is exhausted it still drains the socket into a discard buffer, and either a drop or truncated datagram advances the continuity epoch. The error string is protected by a mutex while atomic flags and counters communicate failure and continuity across the receiver and consumer threads.

sections.title: Copy a bounded depth view
sections.explanation: fill_depth_snapshot validates the requested depth against the fixed maximum and resets the output object before filling it. It copies status and counters, then asks the book to populate bounded bid and ask spans. Explicit counts and symbol presence keep a consumer from interpreting unused array entries as valid liquidity.

sections.title: Own worker and recovery state
sections.explanation: The handler constructs network runtime, ring storage, and the receiver before starting the receiver thread. Its finish helper sets the shared stop flag and joins the thread on every returned outcome. Local state tracks the accepted continuity epoch, expected sequence, current session, and bounded recovery attempts, while observer rejection is treated as a real failure.

sections.title: Accept only a coherent snapshot
sections.explanation: Recovery publishes snapshotting or recovering state and captures the ring continuity epoch before and after GLIMPSE. If the receiver lost data during the snapshot, the candidate is rejected and retried rather than installed. A successful snapshot replaces the local book and establishes the expected next ITCH sequence; authentication and unsupported-message failures remain fatal.

sections.title: Stitch a contiguous live sequence
sections.explanation: A changed receiver epoch triggers another recovery, and a new Mold session or forward sequence gap does the same. Messages older than the recovery boundary are skipped, but every applied message must equal the expected next sequence. Slots are released on success and on handled errors, preventing one malformed packet from permanently occupying bounded storage.

sections.title: Publish termination and failure
sections.explanation: End-of-session publishes a final terminal state before joining the receiver. Otherwise each completed packet updates live depth, and an external stop publishes stopped. Authentication, network, and other protocol/application failures map to distinct exit outcomes while sharing the same cleanup helper.

In the client tour step, it demonstrates how native feed state can inform routing without itself sending orders.

sections.title: Eligible venue liquidity
sections.explanation: current_level accepts only a live feed with the requested symbol present and trading enabled. Buys inspect asks up to the parent limit, while sells inspect bids down to the limit. A cursor identifies the next level for each venue, allowing the planner to revisit a venue after consuming a level.

sections.title: Price priority and child identity
sections.explanation: The comparison picks the lower ask for buys or higher bid for sells, breaking equal prices with configured venue priority. Child lookup reuses the venue's existing child, and new child identifiers combine parent and venue IDs under the FIX length bound. This keeps the output limited to one aggregated child per venue while making equal-price selection deterministic.

sections.title: Parent and feed preconditions
sections.explanation: plan_route validates parent identifiers, symbol, positive quantity and price, and the two venues' distinct IDs and priorities. Both input feeds must be synchronized before the planner proceeds. A rejected plan therefore cannot be mistaken for a route derived from one current book and one stale book.

sections.title: Consuming the best levels
sections.explanation: The loop selects the best currently eligible venue level and takes no more than its shares or the parent's remaining quantity. It accumulates child quantities with an overflow check, updates the child limit to the worst selected price, and advances that venue's cursor. When no eligible level remains, the plan retains routed totals and the unfilled remainder rather than inventing liquidity.

examples/live_exchange.yml.overview: Configures the local continuous-market demonstration with execution, API, FIX, scheduler, WebSocket, observability, and optional recovery settings.

examples/live_market.py.overview: Runs a deterministic live-market demonstration with separate quoting and taking sessions. Reconciles an exact symmetric price ladder as a seeded midpoint walk changes the target.

README.md.overview: The README is the primary statement of MockX behavior and supported public contracts. It connects order lifecycle and timing guarantees to FIX, REST, WebSocket, and the optional native feed, then documents operation and exact numeric boundaries. Use this opening tour step to establish expected behavior before following its implementation in later steps.

sections.title: Purpose and core guarantees
sections.explanation: MockX is described as a deterministic exchange simulator for strategy testing, with price-time matching and a controlled clock. The opening feature list establishes invariants such as immutable reports, exact arithmetic, generation-qualified identities, and deterministic equal-time ordering. Those guarantees provide the criteria for understanding the engine and integration code later in the tour.

sections.title: Supported FIX order behavior
sections.explanation: The supported FIX message set is deliberately narrow, and REST is reserved for administration and observation. Numeric inputs must fit the instrument grid exactly, while IOC and market remainders never rest. Notice that client IDs are scoped to stable sessions and cancel targets are resolved when processing executes, which makes timing races part of the documented contract.

sections.title: Replacement priority and ownership
sections.explanation: The amendment table distinguishes a same-price reduction, a no-op, a priority-losing price or quantity change, and a request at or below cumulative fills. OrderQty remains total quantity rather than desired leaves, and later requests must reference the latest accepted client revision. Participant ownership is separate from a display alias; encountering self-owned liquidity cancels both remainders without creating a trade.

sections.title: Deterministic ingress and latency
sections.explanation: QuickFIX callbacks capture normalized immutable commands and leave engine mutation to the sequenced workflow. Commands are ordered by simulated receive time and ingress sequence before entering scheduled latency stages. Cancel, fill, and replace races therefore resolve from explicit queue order and configured delays rather than from a gateway snapshot of the book.

sections.title: Application delivery guarantees
sections.explanation: One logical execution report or cancel reject enters a retained per-session FIFO with an immutable payload. Versioned due commands and bounded attempt cycles prevent stale wakeups from reviving exhausted work, while permanent serialization failures remain visible blockers. The documented limit is application-level reliability: successful local QuickFIX submission ends application retries, and ambiguous transport outcomes may still yield a client-visible duplicate.

sections.title: Native feed and recovery contracts
sections.explanation: Committed displayed-order changes map to the supported ITCH add, execute, delete, and reduce messages. Mold sequence numbers count messages, while heartbeat and end markers do not consume sequence positions. GLIMPSE captures the book and next ITCH sequence together, so a consumer can discard older buffered messages and resume at one contiguous recovery boundary.

sections.title: Ownership, clocks, and failure
sections.explanation: MockExchange retains explicit component references and uses the lifecycle coordinator to serialize state-changing operations. External mode requires explicit clock advancement, while realtime mode derives elapsed simulation time from a monotonic anchor with bounded catch-up steps. Unexpected handler failures stop the scheduler generation and retain diagnostics; the documentation explicitly warns that partially changed engine state is not rolled back.

sections.title: Read-only state and streaming data
sections.explanation: The route table separates liveness, readiness, book snapshots, statistics, metrics, and the browser interface. Book numeric values are canonical decimal strings, and unknown symbols return structured errors. A WebSocket begins with the latest immutable snapshot without incrementing sequence, then carries committed action snapshots whose trade list belongs only to that action.

sections.title: Metric scopes and clock units
sections.explanation: Statistics distinguish current-run business values from process-lifetime counters and operational gauges. Session end captures final run statistics before clearing them, whereas Prometheus counters remain monotonic for the process. Simulated latency is measured in milliseconds and elapsed CPU-boundary duration in microseconds, so the two time domains remain distinguishable.

sections.title: Exact boundaries and reproducibility
sections.explanation: Instrument conversion checks divisibility before range, and the matching path uses integer ticks and lots throughout. Public display values retain exact decimal totals; average display prices round the exact ratio once using half-even rounding. Restarting a simulation restores its seed and epoch, while the generation prefix and measured wall-clock durations intentionally remain outside identical replay output.

requirements.txt.overview: Pins Python runtime, QuickFIX, API, persistence, testing, and development dependencies used to install and validate the exchange.

scripts/health_probe.sh.overview: Checks that a named Docker container is running and that its local /healthz endpoint returns HTTP 200.

scripts/wait_for_health.sh.overview: Polls health_probe.sh for both demo exchange containers with a bounded retry count before allowing dependent work to continue.

src/mockx/__init__.py.overview: Marks the MockX Python package used by the simulator and its development consumers.

src/mockx/api.py.overview: This FastAPI facade exposes typed snapshots, operational diagnostics, simulation administration, and browser WebSocket subscriptions around the exchange components. Decimal prices and quantities are rendered as strings from immutable snapshots, while lifecycle gates serialize administration and prevent unstable reads. The API tour step links the public response contracts here to the bounded delivery machinery in websocket_delivery.py.

sections.title: Public snapshot contracts
sections.explanation: The response models distinguish health and readiness from market snapshots, individual trades, heartbeats, and errors. Price and quantity fields use decimal strings, and snapshot messages carry sequence and timestamp information so clients can interpret one immutable view. These models establish the public wire shape before any route code is introduced.

sections.title: Diagnostic scopes and models
sections.explanation: The statistics models expose orders, trades, cancellation and replacement outcomes, scheduler state, persistence health, and transport diagnostics. They distinguish current-run results from process-lifetime counters and operational persistence state, avoiding an implied reset of every counter when a simulation restarts. Latency models also separate measured CPU durations from simulated delays.

sections.title: Administrative request validation
sections.explanation: Session models describe seed orders, run identifiers, generation guards, and final results, including failed-run responses. Time advancement accepts exactly one absolute aware timestamp or positive millisecond increment, normalizing absolute time to UTC. Validation therefore establishes a precise request shape before the lifecycle or scheduler is allowed to change state.

sections.title: Snapshot serialization helpers
sections.explanation: Stable error helpers build the public error envelope, while book and market-data helpers render prices and quantities through the snapshot's instrument. Cached price-level values are converted into fresh exported dictionaries, so response consumers cannot mutate the shared cached representation. Trade data and book depth are assembled from the same immutable snapshot rather than separate live engine reads.

sections.title: ASGI ownership and setup
sections.explanation: ExchangeAPI binds its components, bounded connection registry, browser timing settings, templates, and routes. Its lifespan delegates startup and shutdown to the runtime owner when supplied, while an in-process facade has its own lifecycle path; administrative readiness is gated around those transitions. Request validation errors receive stable sorted paths, CORS uses configured origins, and symbol lookup normalizes names before returning a snapshot or a typed not-found error.

sections.title: Readiness and statistics
sections.explanation: Readiness combines component status, scheduler and lifecycle state, and required persistence health to distinguish core readiness from traffic readiness. A FIX delivery backlog can produce a degraded response while otherwise ready traffic still receives status 200. Statistics assemble current-run results alongside process-lifetime FIX, WebSocket, ITCH, and GLIMPSE diagnostics, including disabled defaults when optional native services are absent.

sections.title: Read gates and HTTP views
sections.explanation: Stable simulation reads reject transitions or failed runs, and administration is separately disabled during startup and shutdown. Book, symbol, statistics, health, readiness, and Prometheus routes then expose their specific contracts through those gates. The HTML book view formats the same snapshot and computes a midpoint with exact decimal arithmetic, including the possible half-tick display digit.

sections.title: WebSocket initial snapshot
sections.explanation: A WebSocket connection validates its symbol before registration, then captures and queues its initial snapshot through the lifecycle snapshot operation. The endpoint waits on both client input and the dedicated sender task, enqueueing a heartbeat when the wait times out. Disconnect and sender completion converge on registry cleanup, so socket output remains the responsibility of the bounded delivery layer.

sections.title: Serialized run administration
sections.explanation: Session start and end call the lifecycle and expose run generation, seeded order identities, and final statistics. Manual advancement is restricted to external-clock mode, checks reversal and configured increment limits, and runs through the lifecycle's administrative serialization path. Failed scheduler or metrics-integrity outcomes produce explicit service-error responses that retain the observed time and progress instead of reporting a successful advance.

sections.title: Generation aware publication
sections.explanation: Broadcasting first checks for subscribers, builds one immutable payload, and enqueues it for the symbol with its sequence. When a lifecycle is present, publication is conditioned on the snapshot's generation still being current. The factory at the end binds an in-process API to initialized components and establishes its lifecycle and readiness state.

src/mockx/cli.py.overview: The command-line entry point selects configuration paths and log verbosity, validates the configuration, and runs MockExchange. It is intentionally a thin boundary around the runtime owner, with configuration failures presented as stable path-addressed issues. The startup tour step begins here when launching Python directly or through the container entry point.

sections.title: Logging policy
sections.explanation: Logging receives a consistent timestamped format at the requested level. QuickFIX and Uvicorn loggers are set to warning, reducing their routine output within this CLI setup. The exchange's own logger remains available for startup and failure reporting.

sections.title: Command line configuration
sections.explanation: Argument parsing exposes the YAML configuration path, optional QuickFIX configuration path, and a constrained log-level choice. The configuration and FIX paths can default from their named environment variables, with a conventional YAML path as the fallback. These arguments select inputs; validation of their contents remains in configuration.py.

sections.title: Run and failure reporting
sections.explanation: The CLI loads the validated configuration, constructs MockExchange, and enters its run method. Keyboard interruption is logged, configuration errors are printed issue by issue with path and code, and unexpected errors retain a traceback. Configuration and unexpected failures exit unsuccessfully, while the module guard makes this function usable through python -m mockx.cli.

src/mockx/configuration.py.overview: Configuration is validated into frozen, strict Pydantic models before runtime components are created. This file defines exact instrument metadata, scheduler and transport bounds, optional service dependencies, and stable path-addressed errors. In the startup tour step, read it between the example YAML and MockExchange to see which assumptions runtime construction can rely on.

sections.title: Strict configuration and errors
sections.explanation: ConfigurationError sorts path-addressed issues, making failures deterministic for CLI reporting. Every section inherits a policy that rejects unknown fields, validates defaults, and freezes model attributes. Shared string and decimal helpers reject empty names, booleans used as numbers, and non-finite decimal values before section-specific checks run.

sections.title: Exact instrument metadata
sections.explanation: Instrument increments must be positive and have at most eighteen decimal places. Display precision defaults to the increment scale and may add padding, but cannot discard precision needed to represent the grid. The post-validation assignments resolve optional precision values once, so downstream instruments receive complete formatting metadata.

sections.title: Latency and runtime controls
sections.explanation: Latency configuration permits either one total network delay or a complete inbound/outbound pair, with bounded per-session overrides. Execution probability, random seed, administrative bind settings, FIX retry limits, and participant mappings are validated alongside scheduler mode and limits. Enabling FIX requires a participant mapping, while the scheduler accepts only external or realtime mode and a positive rate no greater than one.

sections.title: ITCH and snapshot authentication
sections.explanation: ITCH metadata constrains single-byte ASCII fields, and GLIMPSE has an independent enable flag. SoupBinTCP settings bound login and write timeouts, connections, replay age, cached sessions, and bytes. Credentials must fit protocol widths, use printable non-space ASCII, and have case-insensitively unique usernames; normalized credentials and session prefixes match the wire representation.

sections.title: Multicast transport bounds
sections.explanation: MoldUDP64 configuration requires an IPv4 multicast destination and a non-multicast IPv4 interface address. It also bounds packet payload size, heartbeat cadence, TTL, port, and the ASCII session prefix. These checks keep invalid socket and wire settings out of transport startup.

sections.title: Browser timing and queues
sections.explanation: WebSocket settings bound queue capacity, send deadlines, snapshot cadence, staleness detection, polling, and reconnect delays. Numeric timing fields explicitly reject booleans. Cross-field checks require staleness thresholds to exceed heartbeat cadence and the maximum reconnect delay to cover the initial delay, keeping the browser timing contract internally consistent.

sections.title: Persistence resource policy
sections.explanation: QuestDB settings describe bounded records and bytes, batch flushing, retry backoff, overflow policy, request timeout, and shutdown deadline. Enabled persistence requires absolute HTTP(S) write and health origins, and credentials must be supplied together. Buffer capacity must accommodate a batch and the retry cap cannot be shorter than its initial delay; the separate Prometheus model controls metric exposition.

sections.title: Whole exchange constraints
sections.explanation: The root model normalizes instrument symbols and rejects duplicates after normalization, while CORS accepts explicit HTTP(S) origins with no wildcard or path. Optional feed dependencies are checked together: GLIMPSE requires ITCH and SoupBinTCP, and ITCH requires MoldUDP64. ITCH also imposes ASCII symbol widths, a locate-count bound, and exact Price(4) representability on tick sizes.

sections.title: Typed environment overrides
sections.explanation: Only the listed QuestDB environment variables participate in the merge. Values are parsed according to an explicit text, integer, or boolean kind, with invalid values reported against their environment-variable path. The merge copies the input mapping and fills the QuestDB section before model validation, so environment input follows the same final contract as YAML.

sections.title: Loading and reporting failures
sections.explanation: Pydantic errors become stable configuration issues with dotted paths and concise messages. load_config checks file existence, parses YAML with safe_load, and rejects a non-mapping root before applying environment overrides and validation. The result is one validated configuration object; malformed files and invalid values share the error shape consumed by the CLI.

src/mockx/delivery.py.overview: OutboundFixDeliveryQueue retains immutable logical FIX responses independently of the current transport connection. It coordinates per-session FIFO order, versioned due events, bounded retry cycles, and operational statistics under a reentrant lock. This file supports the FIX Ingress and Delivery tour step by showing exactly when a response becomes eligible and what survives reconnects or scheduler resets.

sections.title: Own queue state and bounds
sections.explanation: Construction validates positive retry, attempt-cycle, and delivered-retention limits. Separate maps track immutable records, domain identities, currently armed deadlines, per-session queues, and pending enqueue times. The comments make a key retention rule explicit: permanent failures remain backlog blockers, and pruning delivered payloads must not remove pending work.

sections.title: Deduplicate logical responses
sections.explanation: enqueue derives a domain identity from ExecID or the cancel-reject identifier and checks both retained records and delivered tombstones. A conflicting payload or destination for the same domain identity is rejected rather than silently treated as the same message. New records receive a per-session sequence, are appended to that session FIFO, and have their original simulated deadline armed once.

sections.title: Ignore obsolete due events
sections.explanation: Every armed wakeup receives a new schedule version that never resets. mark_due accepts only the queue-owned current command after its deadline, for an eligible record whose attempt cycle is still available. This makes duplicate and stale scheduled events harmless without allowing them to override a newer retry deadline.

sections.title: Attempt, retry, and complete
sections.explanation: A sender attempt requires the DUE record at the session FIFO head and increments both lifetime and current-cycle counters. Transport failure schedules another simulated retry only while the cycle budget remains, whereas permanent failure keeps a visible blocking record. Successful delivery marks the immutable replacement record delivered, removes its pending deadline and FIFO head, and then invokes bounded delivered-record pruning.

sections.title: Reconnect and reschedule retained work
sections.explanation: A new logon can reset the head record attempt cycle without creating a new logical payload. Scheduler reset discards obsolete due commands and arms fresh versions for retained nonterminal work. Pending original latency is preserved when still in the future, while already-due or retrying work becomes eligible at the current simulated time.

sections.title: Report backlog and enforce FIFO
sections.explanation: snapshot returns immutable operational counts and derives the age of the oldest pending record from wall time. The final guard refuses a sender attempt unless the record is DUE and is the first queued record for its session. This local check prevents callers from bypassing ordering even if they hold a valid delivery identifier.

src/mockx/engine.py.overview: The matching engine owns authoritative orders, price levels, client references, and committed market-data changes. It turns validated commands into exact tick-and-lot mutations, immutable reports, and displayed-order events. This tour step connects the shared domain models to price-time matching, cancellation, and native replacement.

sections.title: Run state and seeded liquidity
sections.explanation: The constructor separates per-symbol books, all known orders, active-order membership, and session-qualified client references. Initial liquidity is built and checked in temporary structures before installation requires an empty engine and the matching identifier scope. Publishing that installed snapshot emits displayed additions and book updates without inventing trades.

sections.title: Admission and delayed processing
sections.explanation: Submission claims a session-qualified ClOrdID, allocates an order identity, and schedules a versioned processing command. Processing ignores missing, terminal, already processed, or superseded orders, so delayed work cannot apply an obsolete action twice. A seeded random draw supplies simulated rejection; accepted work buffers displayed events until matching and local invariant checks finish.

sections.title: Self-cross prevention and timing
sections.explanation: Matching duration is measured with a monotonic clock independently of simulated exchange time. When aggressor and passive orders share a participant, self-trade prevention removes the passive order and cancels both complete remainders before any trade is created. It emits cancellation reports, a displayed deletion, and a separate prevention event, preserving the distinction between prevented quantity and executed quantity.

sections.title: Price-time fill commitment
sections.explanation: The aggressor visits the best opposite price and the first queued order at that level, stopping at its limit price. Both orders and their target statuses are validated before integer quantities are committed through the book accounting methods. Each fill produces a displayed execution, a trade, and separate passive and aggressor report snapshots; the loop therefore preserves per-fill reporting even when one aggressor sweeps several orders.

sections.title: Remainders and displayed references
sections.explanation: Market orders and IOC orders cancel any unexecuted remainder and never enter the resting book. A remaining GTC limit order is added through the book, receives a fresh bounded displayed reference, and emits a displayed addition. The NEW report is reserved for a previously unfilled pending order, while earlier fill reports already describe an order that partially executed.

sections.title: Immutable reports and snapshots
sections.explanation: Trade construction records exact ticks, lots, notional, ownership, and aggressor/passive identities from each committed fill. Execution-report creation delegates to the snapshot factory, allocates a unique execution ID, and removes terminal orders from the active-order set. Market-data snapshots capture book levels and fills under one global publication sequence; a read-only snapshot uses the current sequence without advancing it.

sections.title: Cancellation at execution time
sections.explanation: Cancellation resolves the original client reference against current authoritative state after checking generation and duplicate-request flags. The rejection branches distinguish missing references, foreign sessions, superseded ClOrdIDs, and terminal orders. An accepted cancel removes resting liquidity before canceling the remainder and increments the order version, invalidating delayed initial processing; displayed deletion and market-data publication occur only when liquidity had actually rested.

sections.title: Replacement and queue priority
sections.explanation: Replacement validates the current session reference, participant, live GTC limit status, and permitted fields before mutating liquidity. An unchanged price with nonincreasing total quantity retains queue priority through an in-place resize; a price change or quantity increase removes the old displayed reference, then matches and potentially rests the amended order anew. The accepted revision advances the ClOrdID and version, reports REPLACED before any new fills, and publishes buffered displayed changes after the final invariant check.

sections.title: Rejections and event publication
sections.explanation: Unavailable replacement requests still claim their request ID and receive a snapshot-based cancel reject. The displayed-event helpers either append to the current command buffer or notify immediately when no buffer exists. Both cancel and replace reject factories allocate unique response identities and publish explicit outcome observations, keeping rejected requests observable without applying book mutations.

sections.title: Counts and observer isolation
sections.explanation: Engine gauges derive active orders from the maintained membership set and resting orders and levels from the books. CPU measurements reject reversed monotonic timestamps instead of turning them into plausible durations. Observer callbacks are wrapped in exception handling, so an instrumentation or delivery observer failure is logged without interrupting the engine command at that call site.

src/mockx/fix_fields.py.overview: Projects immutable execution reports and cancel/replace rejects into exact FIX-ready scalar fields, enum codes, and generation-aware public identifiers.

src/mockx/gateway.py.overview: This file translates QuickFIX callbacks into immutable exchange commands and translates domain reports back into FIX messages. It owns the handoff from native callback threads to the asyncio lifecycle, stable session identity, client ID claims, and ordered outbound delivery. In the FIX tour step, follow a new order from parsing through the ingress barrier, then follow its report through the delivery queue.

sections.title: Stable sessions and identities
sections.explanation: QuickFIX settings are parsed into stable SessionID strings, and the registry keeps those identities separate from replaceable live transport objects. Its lock protects registration, stale logout detection, and atomic client order ID claims. Accepted IDs survive disconnects, while bootstrap validation can check an entire group before consuming any identity.

sections.title: Native callback boundary
sections.explanation: FIXApplication collects the engine, lifecycle, normalizer, clocks, and delivery queue, while keeping ingress bookkeeping under a separate lock. Logon replaces the live transport and starts delivery recovery; logout removes only the matching transport. Application messages capture a lifecycle token before dispatching new, cancel, or replace requests, so the callback can reject work that arrived outside an active run.

sections.title: Serialized ingress and barriers
sections.explanation: Lifecycle actions and parsed commands are marshalled onto the owning event loop rather than mutating the engine directly from QuickFIX threads. Submissions receive immutable envelopes and sequence numbers, with one wakeup draining FIFO bursts and yielding between batches. A high-water barrier waits for captured submissions, then the locked drain orders eligible envelopes by receive timestamp and accepted sequence before scheduling receive events.

sections.title: Settling failed trading work
sections.explanation: When metrics integrity fails, queued trading events and detached ingress are rejected and their receipts are settled. Arrival events are deliberately skipped because their paired processing events own the terminal response, preventing duplicate reports for one logical command. The explicit wait path rechecks the lifecycle token under its lock before draining, and lifecycle rejections suppress normal application-send metrics.

sections.title: New order normalization
sections.explanation: NewOrderSingle fields enter the shared OrderNormalizer as raw strings and protocol values, producing exact lot and tick quantities before immutable ingress is accepted. Missing sequence numbers, unusable client IDs, and domain validation failures take distinct rejection paths. At processing time the session claims the client ID before engine submission, and malformed orders that can receive domain reports get terminal immutable rejection snapshots.

sections.title: Cancel and replace stages
sections.explanation: Cancel requests preserve both their new request ID and the original order ID, while replacement requests reuse the exact numeric normalization used for new orders. Once an envelope is processed, its request ID is claimed and a command carries the generation, ingress sequence, owner identity, and duplicate flag into separate arrival and engine-processing latency stages. Parse failures produce protocol or cancel-reject responses with the available request context instead of entering the matching path.

sections.title: FIX serialization and rejections
sections.explanation: Domain reports are serialized only at the transport boundary, using snapshot fields rather than rereading mutable orders. Execution reports copy a bounded template containing only constant fields, then add order-specific identifiers, quantities, prices, and fill data; serialization duration is observed independently. Session and business rejection builders require the relevant reference fields, and FIX market-data requests receive an explicit rejection directing clients toward the REST interface.

sections.title: Logical delivery and deadlines
sections.explanation: Enqueueing a report resolves its immutable destination and logical identity before placing it in the outbound queue. The logical enqueue is recorded before its due event is scheduled, and repeated enqueues do not create another initial deadline. Due events drain the destination FIFO, reconnects begin a bounded retry cycle, and scheduler resets reinstall deadlines for nonterminal delivery records.

sections.title: Ordered delivery attempts
sections.explanation: A per-session drain guard prevents concurrent drains from sending the same FIFO head. Disconnected destinations retain their reports, successful sends advance the queue, and transient transport failures enter retry handling while serialization failures are classified separately. Completion updates delivery metrics and latency bookkeeping for the report generation, keeping an old report from completing a newer run's trace.

sections.title: Starting the native acceptor
sections.explanation: Field helpers preserve exact string values and resolve a usable reference sequence when a malformed header cannot provide one. Session identities require an explicit participant mapping, and FIXGateway compares that mapping with the configured QuickFIX sessions before starting. Startup also requires the native module and an installed event-loop handoff; the gateway then owns the acceptor, file store, logs, and stop operation.

src/mockx/glimpse_encoder.py.overview: Builds immutable GLIMPSE snapshot values and encodes directory, trading-state, resting-order, and end-snapshot messages at one ITCH sequence boundary.

src/mockx/glimpse_service.py.overview: GLIMPSE provides authenticated recovery snapshots over a process-lifetime SoupBinTCP listener. It binds each immutable encoded spin to a simulation generation and keeps interrupted spins in a bounded replay cache. This complements live multicast by giving clients a coherent snapshot and a controlled way to resume an interrupted transfer.

sections.title: Listener and cache ownership
sections.explanation: Cached spins retain encoded messages, byte occupancy, generation, expiration, and an exclusive lease flag. Each connection owns a write lock and its last outbound timestamp so heartbeat traffic and data frames share a serialized writer. The service tracks listener state, connection tasks, generations, and cache occupancy separately from individual simulation runs.

sections.title: Process and run lifetimes
sections.explanation: Starting creates the listener once and exposes bind failures as DEGRADED state. Beginning a run revokes old cached sessions and generation-bound connections, while revoking a particular generation cancels only its associated work. Process shutdown additionally closes the listener and waits for canceled connection tasks within a configured timeout.

sections.title: Authentication and bounded I/O
sections.explanation: Session names use a bounded monotonically increasing serial, and expired cache entries are removed only when they are not leased. Authentication looks up normalized credentials and compares the password with `hmac.compare_digest`. Writes share a connection lock and a drain timeout; login parsing also has one overall deadline, so repeated debug packets cannot indefinitely extend authentication.

sections.title: Constructing a coherent spin
sections.explanation: Fresh-spin creation is serialized and checks both session-count and byte capacity before retaining encoded messages. It obtains the snapshot through the supplied factory, verifies the active generation, and performs encoding in a worker thread. A second generation/state check after that await rejects a run that ended during encoding, and the actual encoded size must match the precomputed capacity estimate.

sections.title: Resume and concurrent transfer
sections.explanation: Resumption requires an existing unleased cache entry from the active generation and a valid sequence within that spin. Data sending checks the generation before each message and terminates with an end-session frame, while separate tasks receive client heartbeats or logout and send server heartbeats. When sender or receiver completes, the service cancels and joins the remaining transfer tasks so connection-specific work does not leak.

sections.title: Login routing and cache release
sections.explanation: The client handler enforces the connection limit, authenticates login, and distinguishes fresh sequence-one requests from cached-session resumes. It records the connection generation before serving the spin and handles protocol errors, disconnects, timeouts, and cancellation through one cleanup path. Completed spins leave the cache, interrupted spins in the active generation become replayable until their TTL expires, and stale-generation entries are removed.

src/mockx/identifiers.py.overview: Allocates deterministic public identifiers scoped by run generation, logical event type and monotonically increasing counters.

src/mockx/instruments.py.overview: Instrument metadata is the boundary between decimal values at interfaces and integer ticks and lots inside the exchange. The file rejects invalid or off-grid values, performs exact notional conversions, and renders stable decimal strings for reports and feeds. In the exact-types tour step, it complements numeric.py by applying arithmetic primitives to each configured symbol.

sections.title: Parsing and formatting foundations
sections.explanation: InstrumentConversionError carries a stable code alongside its message. Decimal parsing rejects missing values, booleans, malformed input, and non-finite values before any grid calculation. A bounded typed cache formats common integer unit values through exact decimal multiplication and ratio formatting.

sections.title: Immutable instrument grids
sections.explanation: Instrument is a frozen record of the symbol, tick and lot increments, and display precisions resolved by configuration. Its shared unit conversion requires an exact multiple of the increment within the supported integer range. Off-grid values and overflow become distinct conversion errors, preserving the reason a public numeric input was rejected.

sections.title: Ticks lots and notionals
sections.explanation: Price and quantity entry points require positive values before converting to ticks or lots. Reverse conversions multiply integer units by the exact configured increment, and notional conversion combines tick and lot units without a floating-point intermediate. The engine can therefore store and match integers while retaining precise interface values.

sections.title: Stable decimal output
sections.explanation: Formatting uses the cache only for suitable exact integer inputs and falls back to the same exact arithmetic for other accepted values. Average price divides filled notional by filled quantity, handles the zero-fill case, and uses configured display precision. Notional precision combines the price and quantity scales so exported values retain their unit meaning.

sections.title: Read only symbol catalog
sections.explanation: InstrumentCatalog copies its input into a read-only mapping and refuses an empty catalog. It can build instruments from validated configuration and normalizes lookup symbols by trimming and uppercasing. Optional lookup and required lookup expose different failure behavior, letting callers choose whether an unknown symbol is expected validation input or an internal error.

src/mockx/itch_delivery.py.overview: ITCHFeedPublisher translates committed displayed-order events into a run-scoped native feed. It owns session naming, startup announcements, heartbeat scheduling, degradation, and orderly end markers while delegating byte encoding and datagram transport. The Native ITCH Publication tour step follows this lifecycle around the same exact order-book state used by FIX and WebSocket consumers.

sections.title: Identify and degrade a feed
sections.explanation: The Mold session name combines a padded prefix with an eight-digit generation, and the next message sequence comes from the transport. Send results update message and packet counters separately. A transport or encoder failure stops the transport and publishes DEGRADED once, preserving the error for diagnostics rather than continuing an incoherent stream.

sections.title: Announce a fresh run
sections.explanation: Bootstrap messages announce start-of-messages, instrument directories, system hours, trading state, and market hours in a fixed order. start_run replaces the old transport, resets tracking state, starts the new session, and sends those announcements before marking the feed READY. It schedules a generation-qualified heartbeat event only after successful startup; exceptions take the explicit degradation path.

sections.title: Encode committed displayed changes
sections.explanation: The initial-book context collects seed messages so they can be packetized together before exposing the recovery cut. publish ignores events for another generation or an unavailable feed, then maps added, executed, deleted, and reduced displayed orders to their corresponding ITCH messages. Executions select the price-bearing form only when execution price differs from the displayed price, and failures degrade the publisher.

sections.title: Heartbeat on simulated time
sections.explanation: Heartbeat handling checks both READY state and the event generation before acting. An interval containing data suppresses an extra heartbeat; an idle interval can send a control packet without consuming a message sequence. The next heartbeat is scheduled through the simulator, so its cadence follows simulated advancement rather than a separate wall-clock timer.

sections.title: End coherently and retain diagnostics
sections.explanation: A healthy run emits end-of-market-hours, end-of-system-hours, end-of-messages, and the Mold end-of-session control packet. The finally block always stops and detaches the transport and clears active generation/session state. A degraded state remains visible, while shutdown explicitly transitions to STOPPED and diagnostics preserve cumulative session, send, heartbeat, and failure counters.

src/mockx/itch_encoder.py.overview: The encoder converts exchange identifiers, exact prices, quantities, and timestamps into ITCH 5.0 message bytes. It checks protocol widths and representation boundaries before packing network-order fields, without owning multicast sockets or sequencing delivery. In the native-feed tour step, these builders explain the wire payloads consumed by the ITCH publisher and snapshot service.

sections.title: Exact wire primitives
sections.explanation: ASCII helpers enforce fixed field widths, integer helpers reject booleans and overflow, and quantity lots map one-for-one to the encoded share count. Price conversion derives an exact Price(4) multiplier from the instrument tick size and checks the allowed displayed price range. A bounded cache accelerates valid common multipliers without converting an unbounded decimal exponent into an enormous integer.

sections.title: Timestamp and locate context
sections.explanation: Timestamps must be timezone aware and are normalized to UTC before being encoded as six-byte nanoseconds since midnight. The encoder retains the locate mapping and instrument catalog needed by each message builder. Iteration is ordered by locate code and symbol, making directory emission order explicit rather than dependent on incidental mapping order.

sections.title: Session and directory messages
sections.explanation: System-event, stock-directory, and trading-action builders prepend the ITCH type and common locate, tracking, and timestamp fields. Each builder validates its protocol-sized fields before concatenating packed bytes. Directory messages communicate instrument metadata, while trading actions carry trading state independently of book mutations.

sections.title: Adding visible orders
sections.explanation: Add-order builders encode reference number, side, share count, symbol, and exact Price(4) price. The attributed variant appends a four-byte MPID field while using the same quantity and price boundaries. Both require a domain Side value, so an unrecognized side cannot silently become a buy or sell on the wire.

sections.title: Execution payload variants
sections.explanation: Execution builders tie an order reference and executed shares to a match number. The price-bearing variant adds an explicit execution price and printable flag, while the simpler variant uses the order's established price context. Keeping these layouts separate makes their different wire fields visible to callers.

sections.title: Removing and replacing liquidity
sections.explanation: Cancel and delete messages represent partial quantity removal and complete reference removal respectively. Replacement carries old and new references with a new share count and price, preserving the protocol distinction from a simple size reduction. Each layout checks integer widths and reuses the exact price conversion where a price field is present.

sections.title: Trade and correction messages
sections.explanation: The remaining builders encode non-cross trades, cross trades, and broken-trade notifications. Their layouts differ in reference and quantity fields, including the wider quantity field for cross trades. These are encoding capabilities; deciding when a message is emitted belongs to the publisher that calls the encoder.

src/mockx/latency.py.overview: This module implements simulated time as an ordered event queue and keeps real elapsed-time measurement separate. Order arrival, engine processing, and report delivery become explicit events whose ordering can be reproduced. The tour uses this file to explain equal-time FIFO behavior, inclusive advancement, and terminal failure diagnostics.

sections.title: Exact time and diagnostic values
sections.explanation: Timezone-aware datetimes are converted to integer nanoseconds using integer day, second, and microsecond arithmetic. Diagnostic metadata copies scalar values into sorted immutable tuples instead of retaining mutable command payloads. A separate monotonic-clock protocol measures real durations, and reversed readings raise an error rather than silently producing a duration.

sections.title: Scheduler state and failure
sections.explanation: The scheduler starts at a fixed UTC epoch with a queue, handler registry, generation counter, and per-advancement event budget. Scheduling and advancement require a RUNNING state; the first failed event records its identity, immutable metadata, cause, and failure status before moving the generation to FAILED. Observer errors are isolated, while subsequent work raises the preserved scheduler failure.

sections.title: Stable event insertion
sections.explanation: Every inserted event receives a monotonically increasing sequence and an ID qualified by scheduler generation. The heap stores the scheduled timestamp together with that sequence, providing the data needed to preserve insertion order at equal times. Extracting selected event types sorts the returned events and rebuilds the retained heap without renumbering either group.

sections.title: Arrival and delivery stages
sections.explanation: Order, cancel, and replace helpers schedule arrival and engine-processing events separately. Arrival combines an explicit inbound delay or half the network delay with the session-specific delay, and engine processing adds its configured delay. Execution reports are scheduled as their own outbound events, retaining engine insertion order when delivery timestamps coincide.

sections.title: Bounded inclusive advancement
sections.explanation: The due-event loop processes timestamps at or before the current simulated time and awaits handlers that return awaitables. Missing handlers, raised exceptions, and event-budget exhaustion produce explicit terminal scheduler failures. `run_until` includes events exactly at its target and shares one budget across all timestamps reached, while `run_until_idle` drains pending work without rewinding to an overdue timestamp.

sections.title: Generation reset and inspection
sections.explanation: Queue clearing, time setting, and pending-event inspection expose the administrative control surface. Reset clears queued work and failure state, advances the generation, restarts event numbering, and restores the fixed epoch. Stopping prevents further work without clearing retained diagnostics, which remain available in the diagnostic snapshot.

sections.title: Optional sampled latency
sections.explanation: A latency profile stores network and engine base delays plus an optional jitter fraction. Jitter is sampled only when a caller provides an RNG and the fraction is positive. Passing an explicitly seeded generator therefore lets a scenario vary latency while retaining control of reproducibility.

src/mockx/lifecycle.py.overview: ExchangeLifecycle coordinates simulation generations across matching, scheduling, persistence, FIX ingress, and market-data delivery. Its lock and published ingress token define the boundaries at which commands and observations may safely proceed. This is the Atomic Session Boundaries tour step: inspect how accepted transitions finish, how stale generation work is rejected, and how failure remains observable.

sections.title: Serialize without interrupting commands
sections.explanation: The serialization context drains broadcasts before taking the same lock used by those broadcasts, then rechecks for intervening output. Persistence notifications are marshaled onto the owner event loop and are honored at command boundaries. The command-depth counter allows a synchronous engine handler to finish before a newly detected metric-loss failure closes the run to further trading.

sections.title: Generation checks and cancellation shielding
sections.explanation: Ingress execution compares the captured token with the current active generation while holding the lifecycle lock. Commands crossing a lifecycle transition are rejected instead of being applied to a replacement run. Accepted start/end tasks are awaited through asyncio.shield, and caller cancellation is re-raised only after the transition has settled and any underlying exception has been retrieved.

sections.title: Accept a session start
sections.explanation: Starting first rejects conflicting active or failed-run states and validates that the next generation can form an ITCH session. Initial-book preparation happens before publishing STARTING. The accepted start runs as a named task under the caller-owned lifecycle lock, with a fallback to STOPPED if cancellation prevents the child from taking its first step.

sections.title: Separate preflight from destructive reset
sections.explanation: The start workflow flushes old metrics, closes prior WebSockets, and validates seed claims before resetting scheduler and engine state. It then installs the new identifier scope, restores pending delivery scheduling, initializes metrics and optional feeds, and only finally publishes ACTIVE. Failures before reset return to STOPPED; failures after reset use the failed-start path because the previous run state can no longer be restored.

sections.title: Finish a run with final statistics
sections.explanation: Session end drains persistence before closing the run, including a second drain when newly detected failure creates more rejection metrics. It revokes recovery sessions and ends ITCH before obtaining the final statistics snapshot. A failed flush leaves the run open in its appropriate prior or failed state; only successful completion clears run_id and publishes STOPPED.

sections.title: Take one coherent recovery cut
sections.explanation: GLIMPSE capture verifies that the request has not crossed a generation transition and that the scheduler and current ITCH session remain coherent. Under the lifecycle lock, it validates each book and copies resting order references, exact leaves, prices, and sides into new snapshot values. The returned book content and next ITCH sequence therefore describe the same cut without retaining mutable engine orders.

sections.title: Advance after the ingress barrier
sections.explanation: Administrative advancement first awaits the captured FIX ingress boundary, then checks the generation again after obtaining the lock. It drains commands through that boundary before invoking the scheduler. Realtime advancement uses the same ordering discipline but caps each catch-up target to the configured chunk, keeping a large wall-clock lag from monopolizing one advancement step.

sections.title: Guard observation across generations
sections.explanation: WebSocket registration captures a token before awaiting the lifecycle lock and rejects registration if that token changed. Broadcast delivery similarly checks the intended generation and permissible lifecycle state inside the lock. These guards keep an old run snapshot from being attached to consumers after a reset.

src/mockx/main.py.overview: MockExchange is the composition and lifetime owner for the engine, scheduler, FIX gateway, API, metrics, and optional native feeds and persistence. It wires scheduled events to domain operations and separates simulated clock advancement from asynchronous network delivery. The startup tour step uses this file to connect validated configuration to the components that run together.

sections.title: Constructing the exchange
sections.explanation: The owner stores runtime and broadcast state, then constructs exact instruments, execution parameters, the deterministic scheduler, metrics, latency tracking, and the matching engine. FIXApplication and ExchangeLifecycle share these objects, with optional QuestDB, ITCH, and GLIMPSE services added from configuration. ExchangeAPI receives the runtime owner so ASGI lifespan can control the same component graph.

sections.title: Wiring scheduled behavior
sections.explanation: Callback registration connects receive, arrival, processing, report delivery, heartbeat, trade, and market-data events to their owners. Trading callbacks pass through lifecycle-controlled execution, while delivery and health observers keep their own responsibilities. This wiring is the bridge from named scheduler events to actual engine work and measured latency stages.

sections.title: Startup and readiness
sections.explanation: Startup is serialized and marks components unready while resources are brought online. Persistence is started and the event-loop handoff is installed before the native FIX acceptor can admit callbacks; optional snapshot service startup and the realtime task also belong here. Readiness is enabled only after initialization succeeds, and a stopped owner is not silently restarted.

sections.title: Coordinated shutdown
sections.explanation: Shutdown first stops accepting trading work and cancels pending snapshot coalescing, then stops native services and realtime scheduling. It closes WebSockets and persistence while updating component states, allowing cleanup to continue across component failures. The lifecycle finishes stopped unless it already records a failure, preserving the distinction between a normal end and an unsuccessful run.

sections.title: Feed and order observers
sections.explanation: ITCH degradation updates API status and revokes the active GLIMPSE generation, preventing snapshot service from continuing on a degraded live feed. Order, cancel, and replace callbacks mark their distinct latency stages and route engine results into metrics and FIX delivery. Execution reports are observed as snapshots, and cancel or replace rejection reports are enqueued through their corresponding paths.

sections.title: Tracking asynchronous broadcasts
sections.explanation: Outstanding broadcast futures are stored under a lock and removed by completion callbacks that also report failures. The drain path wakes a pending coalesced flush and waits on the captured asynchronous work. Shielding those futures during the wait keeps the waiter from cancelling the publication it is trying to drain.

sections.title: Coalescing depth snapshots
sections.explanation: The snapshot flush worker publishes the latest queued snapshot for each symbol after the configured interval or an explicit wake. Queue updates compare generation and sequence, retaining the newer snapshot and arranging only one flush owner. Cross-thread scheduling lets engine callbacks submit publication work to the API loop without duplicating that worker.

sections.title: Trade publication and clock
sections.explanation: Every market snapshot is observed by metrics, but only trade-free depth snapshots are eligible for timed coalescing. A snapshot containing trades is published promptly and displaces an older queued depth view, preserving the trade-bearing message. The realtime scheduler loop derives advancement targets from monotonic time through the lifecycle and records scheduler failures rather than continuing normal advancement.

sections.title: Server and explicit closure
sections.explanation: Uvicorn runs the API whose lifespan starts and stops the exchange components. The run method enters that asynchronous server path, while aclose supports in-process ownership and reports persistence degradation when closing a started exchange. The stop method requests server exit, leaving actual teardown to the same lifespan owner.

src/mockx/metrics.py.overview: This module connects authoritative exchange events to run statistics, process metrics, latency measurements, and persistent records. Its buffered writer provides bounded admission, retained retry batches, and explicit shutdown outcomes, while the collector assigns every logical persisted event a run-qualified identity. The metrics tour step shows how measurement remains observational while permanent record loss still marks a simulation run as incomplete.

sections.title: Immutable persistence records
sections.explanation: MetricRecord stores sorted symbol and column tuples together with the event timestamp and injects a required run ID and positive event sequence. Reserved identity fields cannot be supplied through domain data, and the logical encoded size provides deterministic buffer-capacity accounting. Explicit admission, flush, close, and health types distinguish accepted work from loss or incomplete shutdown; the sink protocol has both no-op and in-memory implementations for disabled persistence and tests.

sections.title: Bounded admission and one worker
sections.explanation: Writer construction validates positive capacities and timing settings and separates the thread-safe admission lock from asynchronous flush and close locks. Capacity includes both queued and in-flight records, and the optional drop-oldest policy can discard only queued records that make room without violating in-flight capacity. Nonblocking admission returns an explicit outcome and signals one event-loop worker, while the awaitable admission path performs only a bounded number of capacity retries.

sections.title: Retained retries and final draining
sections.explanation: Taking a batch moves records into an in-flight slot without releasing their byte accounting; failed or canceled writes restore those same records to the front in FIFO order. Automatic flushing and health probes share the flush lock and recheck a monotonic retry deadline, so repeated wakeups cannot bypass exponential backoff. Successful writes reset recovery state, and failure state records lifetime counts, consecutive counts, and the capped retry delay. Closing first seals admission and stops the worker, then makes a bounded final drain attempt and records the exact unflushed result; health snapshots retain occupancy, oldest-record age, and close outcome for inspection.

sections.title: Run and process measurement scopes
sections.explanation: The collector keeps separate run-local and process-lifetime counters and integer per-symbol quantity totals under a reentrant lock. It also retains identity sets for submissions, reports, rejects, and trades, plus process-level delivery and feed gauges. Starting a persistence run resets its event sequence and records a baseline for writer totals; ending resets run statistics while preserving connected-session state and process collectors.

sections.title: Event-owned exchange counters
sections.explanation: Submission counters belong to first-seen engine order IDs, while execution-report IDs and trade identities prevent duplicate observation from counting the same event twice. Report creation owns order lifecycle counters, and immutable trade events add exact lot and tick-lot totals before formatting persistence fields. Seeded orders enter the accepted-ID set without inventing new request counts, and cancel and replace requests, rejects, and declared outcomes have distinct accounting paths.

sections.title: Delivery and committed-state telemetry
sections.explanation: These observer methods expose connection, scheduler, FIX-delivery, WebSocket, ITCH, and GLIMPSE state without making those gauges authoritative for exchange behavior. Latency observation verifies the metric name, expected simulated-millisecond or real-microsecond unit, and finite nonnegative value before updating aggregates and persistence. Book persistence records complete committed depth including empty sides, with explicit presence and spread-validity flags, while active/resting/level gauges query the engine. Persistence health and baseline-adjusted run outcomes report buffer pressure and loss separately from exchange counters.

sections.title: Exact nonmutating metric snapshots
sections.explanation: Integer per-symbol totals are converted through instrument scales and summed as Decimal values only when physical totals are needed. Process-lifetime snapshots expose cumulative event statistics, while the run snapshot combines copied run counters with current engine gauges and reports absent latency averages as null. Both format quantity and notional totals as decimal strings, and Prometheus export refreshes persistence gauges before serializing the isolated registry.

sections.title: Identity reservation and integrity
sections.explanation: Persistence requires an active run and timestamps that never move backward relative to its event sequence. A new identity is reserved before calling the writer because admission might enqueue the record and then raise; later records must never reuse that uncertain identity. Rejection, dropped-oldest admission, and construction failures preserve the first integrity fault and notify outside the collector lock, allowing lifecycle code to observe incomplete metrics without this observer directly interrupting a book mutation.

sections.title: Generation-qualified simulated traces
sections.explanation: Order traces use generation and order ID, while cancel and replace traces use generation and ingress sequence so requests remain distinct from their target order. First arrival and first report creation define inbound and engine stages, and successful response delivery completes outbound and end-to-end measurements with duplicate guards. Seeded liquidity has no invented submission timestamp; retained replacement traces can carry an explicit clock offset across a run reset. The diagnostic measurement deque is bounded independently of aggregate counters and persisted events.

sections.title: Clock-safe durations and cleanup
sections.explanation: CPU and serialization boundaries convert nonnegative monotonic nanoseconds to microseconds, while simulated trace differences produce milliseconds. Invalid or reversed durations are rejected and counted, and each immutable measurement retains the appropriate report, request, and generation context before publication. Terminal cleanup consults the report snapshot and generation-qualified trace key, and missing traces produce diagnostic warnings instead of fabricated timing values.

src/mockx/models.py.overview: This file defines the exchange vocabulary shared by the engine, scheduler, gateway, and market-data paths. It separates immutable commands and reports from mutable engine-owned orders and books, while keeping authoritative prices and quantities in integer ticks and lots. In the Exact Values and State tour step, follow the checks that connect an order mutation to level totals, lookup indexes, and immutable output.

sections.title: Identity and exact client intent
sections.explanation: SessionIdentity makes the stable session string the routing key, while ClientOrderKey scopes a client identifier to that session.
