NewOrderCommand captures immutable intent and rejects nonpositive or boolean quantities, missing ownership, and invalid price/type combinations. The distinction between descriptive aliases and stable identity is important when sessions reconnect or several sessions share a participant.

sections.title: From callback to ordered ingress
sections.explanation: ParsedFixCommand checks the normalized FIX fields before they enter the exchange workflow. FixIngressEnvelope then adds the simulation generation, receive timestamp, and ingress sequence. Its ordering key explicitly combines time with sequence, so equal-time commands have a deterministic tie-break independent of session names.

sections.title: The mutable order aggregate
sections.explanation: Order stores exact original, filled, canceled, and notional quantities alongside identity and lifecycle state. Construction verifies instrument agreement, positive grid units, and that fills plus cancellations do not over-allocate the original quantity. Liquidity origin is captured once so later status or alias changes cannot move resting quantity between accounting categories.

sections.title: Validate before changing quantities
sections.explanation: The fill preview computes the resulting filled quantity, notional, and leaves before any assignment occurs. apply_fill commits those prevalidated values, while cancellation moves quantity into the canceled counter rather than treating it as execution. State changes also pass through an explicit transition table, making invalid lifecycle jumps observable errors.

sections.title: Keep level totals synchronized
sections.explanation: BookLevel validates both total quantity and the split between strategy and market origin. Resting eligibility requires a live GTC limit order with positive leaves and matching side and price. Fill and self-trade-prevention reductions compute replacement aggregates before mutating the order, then remove fully depleted members from the FIFO queue.

sections.title: Coordinate book indexes and projections
sections.explanation: OrderBook insertion checks duplicate identity and the placement of sorted price levels before updating the order index and immutable level projection. A resting fill first validates membership, location, price, and resulting aggregates. After the level mutation, it removes terminal order/index entries and empty levels, or refreshes the surviving level projection.

sections.title: Recompute independent book invariants
sections.explanation: The full invariant pass walks queues to reconstruct the set of live orders rather than trusting lookup caches. It checks sorted prices, duplicate membership, symbol agreement, best prices, and the strict bid-below-ask condition. It then compares reconstructed order and level locations with both indexes and cached immutable projections, which exposes corruption that a single representation could hide.

sections.title: Publish scalar market snapshots
sections.explanation: PriceLevelSnapshot and TradeSnapshot enforce positive published quantities, valid identity, and coherent timestamps. MarketDataSnapshot ties ordered bid/ask tuples to an instrument, generation, and global sequence. These values describe a committed observation; consumers do not need access to mutable order queues to render the book.

sections.title: Capture reports at creation time
sections.explanation: The report factories copy current scalar order values into a new response object, including cumulative fills, remaining quantity, client revision, and generation. Public order and trade identities receive generation-qualified forms when no explicit identifier was supplied. Cancel and replace rejects use the immutable command plus optional current order state, so delayed transmission cannot silently recalculate the original response.

sections.title: Version deadlines and scheduled work
sections.explanation: FixDeliveryDueCommand carries a schedule version and deadline, allowing the retained delivery queue to distinguish current wakeups from obsolete ones. OutboundFixDelivery records immutable payload identity and separate attempt, retry, and delivery timestamps; its validation checks that the domain identifier matches the payload. ScheduledEvent compares timestamp and sequence, while SchedulerFailure retains scalar diagnostic metadata instead of exposing a live command object.

src/mockx/moldudp64_transport.py.overview: This module owns a downstream IPv4 multicast socket and packs ITCH payloads into MoldUDP64 datagrams. It enforces wire-size limits and advances sequence numbers by data-message count. In the native-feed tour step, it is the final transport boundary below the publisher and encoder.

sections.title: Validated session configuration
sections.explanation: The configuration validates the ASCII session name, multicast group, outgoing interface, port, payload limit, heartbeat interval, and TTL. The session name is padded to the fixed ten-byte wire field. A small asyncio protocol forwards socket lifecycle and error callbacks to the owning transport, while immutable send results report message count, packet count, and the next sequence.

sections.title: Socket and session ownership
sections.explanation: A transport begins with next sequence one and rejects an attempt to start while already active. Startup configures a nonblocking IPv4 UDP socket with its multicast TTL and interface, binds an ephemeral local port, and hands it to asyncio. Shutdown clears the active transport before closing it; errors are logged and forwarded through an isolated callback.

sections.title: Wire framing and limits
sections.explanation: Packet construction validates a positive unsigned 64-bit sequence and writes the session field followed by a big-endian sequence and message count. Each data message is preceded by a two-byte length, while an empty heartbeat uses count zero and end-of-session uses the reserved terminal count. Both individual message size and final datagram size are checked before the packet is returned.

sections.title: Batching and sequence advancement
sections.explanation: Batching prevalidates messages and partitions them according to payload space and the maximum data-message count. Sending requires an active session, checks that the next sequence remains representable, and advances it only after `sendto` returns successfully. Sequence progression is based on messages rather than datagrams, so packets containing several ITCH messages consume several sequence positions.

sections.title: Control packets and diagnostics
sections.explanation: Heartbeat and end-session sends return false when no session is active and consume no data sequence positions. Capacity helpers account for both the MoldUDP64 header and each message-length prefix. Diagnostics expose the configured multicast destination, session name, current activity, and the next expected message sequence.

src/mockx/numeric.py.overview: Numeric helpers preserve finite decimal boundaries without relying on the calling thread’s Decimal precision or rounding settings. They convert exact decimal coefficients into bounded integral units and produce canonical display values. In Exact Values and State, this file explains how decimal wire text can enter an integer matching engine without hidden rounding.

sections.title: Work with coefficient and exponent
sections.explanation: Parsing preserves decimal text, while _parts rejects nonfinite input and separates the signed coefficient from its decimal exponent. Optional normalization removes trailing zeros without using ambient Decimal normalization. Rebuilding from a tuple preserves an explicit scale and, where requested, negative zero, so later arithmetic can remain coefficient-based.

sections.title: Check the grid before range
sections.explanation: bounded_units first reduces the value-to-increment ratio by a greatest common divisor. It verifies that the remaining denominator can be canceled by powers of two and five before checking the maximum unit count. This preserves an off-grid rejection even for extreme exponents and avoids expanding huge powers merely to discover that the value was never an integral number of ticks or lots.

sections.title: Accumulate exact decimal totals
sections.explanation: Products multiply integer coefficients and add exponents. Sums align coefficients to the smaller exponent before adding them. Both paths reconstruct Decimal values directly, retaining exact significant digits and scale without a context-rounded intermediate result.

sections.title: Round display ratios once
sections.explanation: format_decimal_ratio scales an exact numerator and uses integer division and remainder to implement half-even rounding at the requested display precision. It handles tiny values and signed zero explicitly, then formats a fixed-scale string. average_decimal is a separate derived-value helper with an explicit 28-significant-digit context, so that potentially approximate average does not replace exact authoritative totals.

src/mockx/questdb_writer.py.overview: This adapter implements the metrics sink using acknowledged QuestDB ILP over HTTP and explicit SQL-managed schemas. Each table uses the logical metric identity as part of its deduplication key, so distinct events sharing a timestamp remain distinct and retries can refer to the same event. The tour places this file after the buffered writer because it owns transport and schema verification rather than queue admission policy.

sections.title: Schemas and event identity
sections.explanation: The schema helper combines shared identity columns with explicit symbol, integer, floating, boolean, and text columns for each metric table. DDL requires a designated timestamp, daily partitioning, WAL, and deduplication on timestamp, run ID, and metric-event sequence. Exact order and trade quantities remain integer columns with separately formatted text fields, while book snapshots carry explicit validity flags and serialized depth.

sections.title: Acknowledged client configuration
sections.explanation: Construction requires the optional QuestDB client and a positive request timeout, then accepts only an absolute HTTP or HTTPS ingestion URL. Sender auto-flush and internal retries are disabled, leaving batch boundaries and retry policy visible to the outer buffered writer. Initialization creates both ingestion and SQL/health clients and closes any partially constructed resources if setup fails.

sections.title: Explicit writes and health probes
sections.explanation: A write first ensures the schemas, fills a fresh sender buffer from immutable metric records, and flushes that buffer explicitly. Blocking sender and HTTP operations run under a shared thread lock, preventing schema checks, writes, and health probes from racing on client state. SQL responses must be mappings without a reported error, and their column metadata is paired with rows for subsequent verification.

sections.title: Verifying the database contract
sections.explanation: Verification checks the designated timestamp, day partitioning, WAL, and enabled deduplication in table metadata. It then compares the complete actual column-type mapping with the expected schema and requires the exact deduplication-key set. Creating a table if absent is therefore insufficient by itself: an existing incompatible table fails validation rather than silently accepting a different persistence contract.

sections.title: Timeouts and orderly closure
sections.explanation: Closure is serialized, executes blocking cleanup in a worker thread, and closes the sender without an implicit flush. If both sender and HTTP cleanup fail, the first sender failure is preserved. The shared operation wrapper imposes a timeout and invalidates the schema-ready cache on errors, ensuring a later retry rechecks the database before writing.

src/mockx/soupbintcp_transport.py.overview: This module implements SoupBinTCP logical framing and the fixed-width login/control fields used by GLIMPSE. It keeps packet bytes and parsed login values separate from listener lifecycle and authentication policy. In Recovering a Feed Snapshot, read it to understand why TCP chunk boundaries cannot be treated as application-message boundaries.

sections.title: Define logical packet values
sections.explanation: The constants name the one-byte Soup packet types, rejection reasons, and fixed length limits. Frozen SoupPacket values require an exactly one-byte type and a byte payload. LoginRequest holds decoded credential, session, sequence, and heartbeat fields for the service layer to interpret.

sections.title: Validate fixed-width ASCII fields
sections.explanation: Encoding helpers enforce ASCII, width, allowed characters, and the required left or right padding convention. Decoding performs corresponding checks and rejects interior spaces or nondigit sequence fields. These checks keep malformed credential/session text from being silently normalized into another valid request.

sections.title: Frame and parse login requests
sections.explanation: encode_packet prefixes the type-plus-payload length as an unsigned big-endian 16-bit field. Login construction uses fixed credential/session/sequence widths plus the heartbeat field and enforces its permitted range. Parsing requires the login packet type and exactly 51 payload bytes before slicing the same field boundaries.

sections.title: Encode session control responses
sections.explanation: Login acceptance requires a nonempty session and positive next sequence; login rejection accepts only the defined reason codes. Sequenced data, unsequenced data, debug, heartbeat, logout, and end-session helpers all reuse the same packet framing primitive. The shared encoder makes their length behavior consistent even when the payload is empty.

sections.title: Reassemble arbitrary TCP chunks
sections.explanation: SoupPacketParser appends bytes to a private buffer and emits complete logical packets as long as their full length is available. An incomplete packet remains buffered across calls, so one TCP read may contain part of a message or several messages. finish rejects a trailing fragment instead of silently accepting a truncated stream.

sections.title: Read one complete packet
sections.explanation: The async reader requests exactly two length bytes and then exactly the announced body length. A zero logical length is rejected before body interpretation. This provides a direct stream-reader path with the same type/payload boundary as the incremental parser.

src/mockx/validation.py.overview: Normalizes untrusted order terms into immutable commands with participant identity, supported order semantics, and exact tick/lot validation.

src/mockx/websocket_delivery.py.overview: This module isolates each WebSocket subscriber behind a bounded outbound buffer and a single sender task. It gives the initial snapshot special treatment, conflates later depth updates, and handles slow or disconnected peers without making every broadcast perform network I/O. The API tour step pairs this delivery machinery with the subscription endpoint in api.py.

sections.title: Frames and bounded state
sections.explanation: Explicit connection states, frame kinds, and enqueue outcomes describe the delivery state machine. OutboundBuffer owns a bounded deque, wake event, depth observer, and latest accepted sequence. Immutable frame records distinguish market data from heartbeat, fatal error, and close work before the sender touches the socket.

sections.title: Initial snapshot and conflation
sections.explanation: The initial market snapshot is queued once and is not a candidate for later snapshot replacement. Later snapshots with stale sequences are ignored, while newer ones replace an existing noninitial market frame or evict a heartbeat when capacity is needed. This preserves the subscription baseline while bounding the backlog of intermediate depth views.

sections.title: Heartbeat and fatal frames
sections.explanation: Heartbeats replace an already queued heartbeat or are dropped when the buffer has no room. Fatal-error handling clears obsolete work while retaining a pending initial snapshot, then queues the error and a close frame when capacity permits. The asynchronous get operation waits on the buffer event and reports depth changes as frames leave.

sections.title: Atomic subscriber registration
sections.explanation: A connection owns its buffer, sender task, counters, and cleanup lock, while the registry indexes connections globally and by symbol. Registration queues the initial snapshot under the registry lock before exposing the connection as active and starting its sender. That ordering prevents an ordinary broadcast from becoming the first frame a new subscriber sees.

sections.title: Enqueueing subscriber updates
sections.explanation: Registry snapshots and counts use the registry lock, while market-data fanout enqueues into each active subscriber's buffer. Conflated and dropped outcomes update per-connection and process metrics. Heartbeats use the same buffer rather than competing with the sender through direct writes.

sections.title: One bounded socket sender
sections.explanation: Only the sender loop removes frames and calls the WebSocket transport. Each JSON send has a timeout; slow sends and transport errors trigger cleanup with distinct close reasons and metric outcomes. Successful sends update last-send information, while fatal error delivery terminates the connection through the same cleanup path.

sections.title: Idempotent connection cleanup
sections.explanation: Detachment removes registry membership and updates connection metrics once under the registry lock. A separate per-connection cleanup lock coordinates buffer clearing, sender cancellation, bounded socket closure, and the final CLOSED state. Cleanup detects when it is running inside the sender itself, avoiding self-cancellation or waiting on its own task.

sections.title: Closing all subscribers
sections.explanation: Global shutdown first detaches every registered connection under the registry lock. It then runs their cleanup concurrently and gathers exceptions, allowing one failed socket close to coexist with completion of the other closes. No new broadcast can discover those detached connections while cleanup is in progress.

sections.title: Independent quantity reference
sections.explanation: The order helper constructs explicit limit orders with separate participant identities. The reference check recomputes level totals from queued order leaves and separates strategy quantities from other liquidity instead of trusting cached aggregates. This gives the tests an independent comparison for the accounting maintained by BookLevel.

sections.title: Proving corruption is detected
sections.explanation: Focused tests damage a level total, bypass the queue's duplicate guard, move quantity between liquidity categories, and leave an empty level behind. Other cases construct crossed or locked best prices and assert that the invariant checker rejects them. These tests verify the checker itself, including diagnostic context, before relying on it in larger histories.

sections.title: Deterministic engine fixture
sections.explanation: The history fixture builds an engine with two exact instruments, zero configured latency, and a fixed execution seed. This keeps scheduling and random rejection effects controlled while exercising book operations. Symbol-specific metadata remains present, so the checks still use the same instrument-aware engine boundary as other code.

sections.title: Seeded command history
sections.explanation: A fixed random seed drives a long sequence of resting orders, crossing orders, cancellations, and repeated cancellation attempts. After every command, the test checks book invariants, recomputed aggregates, and the absence of empty levels. Failure output includes the seed, step, and recent command history, making a stochastic-looking failure reproducible.

sections.title: Generated invariant properties
sections.explanation: Hypothesis generates bounded lists of submission and cancellation operations, including GTC and IOC behavior. Each operation is followed by checks that both sides remain strictly uncrossed, live orders have allowed states, and terminal orders are absent. Market and IOC orders are also checked for non-resting behavior, tying generated histories directly to the exchange's core rules.

sections.title: Generated command histories
sections.explanation: Hypothesis generates up to fifty commands per example and explores fifty examples without a wall-clock deadline. The engine uses exact helper instruments, zero configured delays, a fixed random seed, and a generation-specific identifier scope. The test keeps separate original client IDs, a displayed-book reconstruction, and all previously used displayed references.

sections.title: Revisions and stale references
sections.explanation: Generated actions submit new GTC limits or select an existing order for replacement or cancellation. Some requests deliberately reference the original ClOrdID instead of the current revision, exercising rejection paths alongside accepted mutations. Unique request IDs and explicit generation/ingress values make each generated action identifiable while ownership follows the selected order.

sections.title: Independent displayed-book oracle

It checks that references are never reused and displayed quantities never become negative. After every command it runs book invariants, compares active and resting counts, requires exact equality between reconstructed displayed liquidity and resting orders, and verifies that every terminal order is absent from the book.
